title: Does High-Frequency Consumption Data Predict Equity Risk Premiums?
affiliations: INTAGE Inc., Hokkaido University and aiQ Inc

detail.title: Does High-Frequency Consumption Data Predict Equity Risk Premiums?

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by Japan Society for the Promotion of Science KAKENHI Grant Number 24K16398

detail.abstract: This study employs a novel consumption dataset from Japan to investigate whether fluctuations in consumption are associated with future equity risk premiums at a weekly frequency. We find that negative consumption growth rates are associated with higher equity risk premiums in the Japanese market indices. This pattern is observed across large-and small-cap indices, as well as industry indices, which are traded by different types of investors. We also propose market timing strategies based on our consumption growth rates. These strategies increase the Sharpe ratio by 0.27 per annum. In addition, our results suggest that the consumption of nondurable goods plays an important role in time-varying risk premiums.

title: Energy Shock Spillovers in European Polycrises: Evidence on Inequality Impacts and Policies for Clean Energy Transition
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice

detail.title: Energy Shock Spillovers in European Polycrises: Evidence on Inequality Impacts and Policies for Clean Energy Transition
detail.abstract: Europe faces interconnected risks from environmental shocks, such as energy price surges and climate events, which amplify inequality during polycrises. This study integrates objective proxy data (2000–2025), including Eurostat energy prices and Gini coefficients, EM-DAT climate events, and GPR geopolitical indices, into a network-augmented stochastic dynamic model, combined with panel TVP-VAR analysis, to examine spillovers from environmental risks to economic and societal domains. Empirical results show that energy shocks increase economic risk by 32% during crises, widening inequality by 28% through channels like financial frictions and reduced consumption for low-income households. Simulations of a European energy shock project a 36% rise in economic risk and 30% in inequality by year 5. Policy interventions, such as carbon tariffs and monetary tightening, mitigate amplification by 42%. This framework provides tools for EU environmental policy to enhance equity and resilience in the clean energy transition.

title: Gender and Digital Platform Work during Turbulent Times
affiliations: Independent Researcher and Rutgers University - School of Management and Labor Relations

detail.title: Gender and Digital Platform Work during Turbulent Times
detail.abstract: This commentary explores how the platform economy shapes labour market responses during times of crisis, with a focus on gendered experiences. Drawing on cases of economic crisis, natural disasters, and refugee displacement, it examines how digital labour platforms offer flexible work opportunities while also reinforcing existing inequalities. Women face distinct constraints-such as caregiving responsibilities, limited mobility, and economic insecurity-that hinder their employment opportunities and earnings potential. These constraints are more pronounced during crises, when access to stable income and safe working conditions becomes more difficult. While platform work can serve as a lifeline, it is not a guaranteed solution, and its benefits are unevenly distributed. The commentary calls for gender-responsive policies and new research to understand how digital infrastructures mediate labour experiences across different crisis contexts. Such research can inform inclusive strategies that promote resilience and equity in platform-based work, particularly for marginalized and displaced populations.

title: Consumption and Non-Payment Responses to Retail Electricity Prices in India
affiliations: Imperial College London and Uber

detail.title: Consumption and Non-Payment Responses to Retail Electricity Prices in India
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the long-run responses of retail electricity consumption and bill payment to electricity prices in Delhi, India from 2015 to 2019. Using billing data from one of Delhi's three private electricity distribution utilities, we reconstruct payment histories for more than 1.5 million residential, commercial, and small industrial customers. Our empirical strategies exploit features of the regulated electricity price schedule that generate long-run variation in the average price of electricity for these customers. In addition to providing annual price elasticity estimates, we find evidence that non-payment rates increase when prices rise. The effects are particularly large for the poorest informal customers, for whom arrears more than double in response to a doubling in the average electricity price.

title: Beyond Monotonicity: The Nonlinear Effects of Industry Competition on Corporate ESG Performance and Energy Choices
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU),  and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business

detail.title: Beyond Monotonicity: The Nonlinear Effects of Industry Competition on Corporate ESG Performance and Energy Choices
detail.abstract: This study theorizes and tests a nonlinear relationship between industry concentration and corporate ESG performance. We construct a symmetric game-theoretic model to predict and to empirically validate an inverted U-shaped relationship using data from Chinese A-share listed firms (2010–2024). A key finding reveals significant heterogeneity across ESG dimensions: the Environmental dimension exhibits a positive linear relationship with concentration, driven by scale and regulation, while the Social and Governance dimensions follow an inverted U-shape, consistent with strategic motives. Mechanism analyses confirm that strategic differentiation, reputational pressure, and resource capacity underpin this relationship. We also find an inverted U-shaped (U-shaped) relationship between industry concentration and the use of clean (polluted) energy, validating our theoretical model and offering direct insights for energy and climate policy. Our findings reveal a nonlinear relationship and provide a unified framework with critical implications for fostering moderate competition and targeted ESG regulation.

title: Asset Valuation Fundamentals for Deregulated Energy Markets: The Present Cost Of Energy, Standard Formulation
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Asset Valuation Fundamentals for Deregulated Energy Markets: The Present Cost Of Energy, Standard Formulation
detail.abstract: Energy infrastructure projects involve high upfront capital expenditures, long payback periods, and varying risk exposure over their lifetime. Over the past four decades, particularly in the U.S., financing has shifted from public to private capital, increasing exposure to capital market risks and requiring greater efficiency. Despite this, the levelized cost of energy (LCOE), originally created for utilities overseeing development, operation, and transmission, remains widely used for planning, strategy, and policymaking. LCOE has key methodological limitations: it excludes variability in project risk and its effect on the cost of capital, overlooks revenue escalation, variable cost escalators, and lacks comparability to present market prices. To address these issues, the present cost of energy (PCOE) formulation is proposed. PCOE incorporates empirical cost and revenue escalation, cost of capital variability, asset operational degradation, and projected technology learning and cost reduction. Comparing PCOE with LCOE reveals significant discrepancies that vary across generators. Evaluated technologies include large-scale nuclear, combined-cycle gas turbines, coal, utility-scale solar photovoltaic, and onshore wind. They are assessed under three market scenarios: a free market, project guarantees for clean energy technologies, and a combination of guarantees with investment tax credits. Results show natural gas assets as superior under free market conditions, with nuclear and renewables behind but comparable. Project guarantees benefit technologies with long construction timelines by reducing financing during construction. Investment tax credits improve the competitiveness of nuclear and renewables projects in the U.S. becoming in some cases, more competitive than natural gas.

title: Total Factor Productivity is fully explained by changes in physical energy efficiency: an exergy economics approach
affiliations: , Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária (INIAV, I.P.) - MARETEC and Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária (INIAV, I.P.) - MARETEC

detail.title: Total Factor Productivity is fully explained by changes in physical energy efficiency: an exergy economics approach
detail.abstract: Aggregate final-to-useful exergy efficiency captures how effectively final energy is converted into useful exergy – where most thermodynamic losses occur – that delivers economic services e.g. heat, motion, and light. Because gains at this stage reflect genuine technological progress in physical production efficiency, we assess whether changes in final-to-useful efficiency provide a measurable explanation for historical total factor productivity (TFP), extending earlier evidence that such gains account for much of observed productivity improvements.We compute four TFP measures using quantity-based and quality-adjusted inputs for Austria 1960-2020 and estimate 100 possible VECM specifications combining five lag orders with five deterministic term structures: no constant/trend; restricted constant; unrestricted constant; unrestricted constant+restricted trend; unrestricted constant+unrestricted trend. After Bonferroni correction, the only four statistically valid models all correspond to the restricted-constant, no-trend specification, with elasticities of 0.35–0.94.This specification isolates the long-run TFP-efficiency equilibrium without attributing growth to independent trends, while ensuring observed co-movements are not driven by spurious correlations, and confirms that improvements in exergy efficiency account for a substantial share of Austria’s historical TFP. Efficiency being thermodynamically bounded, our findings suggest limits to future productivity growth and climate-economic projections that assume exogenous, unconstrained TFP. Integrating this measurable link into IAMs and growth-policy frameworks would yield more realistic long-run output trajectories.

title: Risk Spillover Effects of Climate Policy Uncertainty on Global Energy Markets: A Time–Frequency Perspective
affiliations: Shandong University of Finance and Economics and Shandong University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Risk Spillover Effects of Climate Policy Uncertainty on Global Energy Markets: A Time–Frequency Perspective
detail.abstract: This study examines how climate policy uncertainty influences risk spillovers across global energy markets from both time and frequency perspectives. Using wavelet coherence, we first describe the localized time varying relationship between CPU and major energy prices and identify periods of stronger co-movement as well as shifts in the direction of influence. A time varying parameter VAR model combined with generalized forecast error variance decomposition and the Diebold and Yilmaz connectedness index is then used to measure spillovers in the time dimension. The results show that CPU increases overall connectedness and creates an asymmetric pattern in which traditional energy markets tend to transmit more risk to clean energy markets. The frequency analysis based on the Barunik and Krehlik decomposition further indicates that short term spillovers intensify during periods of elevated policy uncertainty, whereas longer term linkages become more pronounced when policy conditions are relatively stable. These findings suggest that climate policy uncertainty is an important source of systemic risk for global energy markets and provide useful implications for policymakers concerned with the stability of energy transition and for investors managing exposures across different energy sectors.

title: Reducing CO2 emissions: Goodness of heart or insurance policy?
affiliations: Memorial University of Newfoundland (MUN) - Faculty of Business Administration, Memorial University of Newfoundland (MUN), Audencia Business School and Macquarie University - Department of Accounting and Corporate Governance

detail.title: Reducing CO2 emissions: Goodness of heart or insurance policy?
detail.abstract: We examine how firm-level political risk shapes corporate carbon emissions. Heightened political risk is associated with lower emissions, consistent with the Risk-Mitigation Hypothesis. Exploiting Trump’s unexpected 2016 election as an exogenous shock in a difference-in-differences setting, we show that the reduction in emissions is concentrated among heavy emitters in the post-election period compared to low-emitting and compared to pre-election period firms. Additional tests indicate that this effect is moderated by an “insurance policy”: politically connected and socially responsible firms do not significantly curtail emissions. We also document a governance channel whereby CEO compensation declines when firms maintain high emissions under political uncertainty, aligning managerial incentives with emissions reduction. Overall, our evidence suggests that emissions reductions are not automatic responses to political risk but depend on managerial characteristics, and that firms approach emissions strategy as operational hedging rather than purely voluntary environmental engagement.

title: Politicization of Curriculum and the Erasure of National Memory in Bangladesh's Education System

detail.title: Politicization of Curriculum and the Erasure of National Memory in Bangladesh's Education System
detail.abstract:
The curriculum of any nation functions as a central instrument for transmitting knowledge, shaping identity, and defining collective memory. In Bangladesh, however, curriculum design has become a contested political arena in which ruling regimes attempt to reshape, erase, or selectively emphasize elements of national history. This article critically investigates how political influence over Bangladesh’s education curriculum contributes to the erosion of national memory, especially
regarding the Liberation War, secular ideals, contributions of historical leaders, and minority narratives. Using a mixed‐method approach—textual analysis of textbooks, secondary historical documents, policy papers, and qualitative interviews—this study demonstrates the structural patterns through which political regimes embed ideology into educational materials. The findings reveal extensive politicization manifested in selective historical representation, removal of  progressive literary icons, glorification of regime-aligned political actors, and the diminishing of pluralistic identities. The article argues that such manipulation constitutes a form of ‘memory warfare’ where the curriculum becomes a tool for manufacturing consent and legitimizing regimes. The study concludes with implications for democratic citizenship, academic freedom, and the
safeguarding of national identity in Bangladesh.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Corporate Default Risk
affiliations: Beijing Technology and Business University, Beijing Technology and Business University, Central University of Finance and Economics and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Corporate Default Risk
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a key driver of enterprise digital transformation, deeply integrated into corporate operations and management. However, the relationship between AI adoption and corporate default risk remains underexplored. Using a sample of Chinese listed companies from 2009 to 2023, we examine the impact of AI adoption on corporate default risk. The findings reveal a significant negative association between AI adoption and default risk, suggesting that greater AI adoption corresponds with lower default probabilities and larger default distances. AI enhances corporate resilience by increasing R&D expenditure, stimulating patent output, improving corporate social responsibility performance, reducing overhead costs, and enhancing asset efficiency. The risk-mitigating effect of AI adoption is stronger in firms facing higher media scrutiny, heavier tax burdens, and greater regional social trust. Overall, the results highlight the critical role of AI adoption in strengthening financial management and risk control.

title: Women's Rights at Jeopardy: An Overview of Sexual Violence Perpetrated Against Women During Armed Conflict with Special Reference to the Russia-Ukraine War

detail.title: Women's Rights at Jeopardy: An Overview of Sexual Violence Perpetrated Against Women During Armed Conflict with Special Reference to the Russia-Ukraine War
detail.abstract: The wake of world wars and armed conflicts reiterated the vulnerability of women and the severity of violence perpetrated against them. Women have always been subjected to sexual violence, whether during peacetime, prewar , or postwar times. However, the gravity of the violence is barbarous in times of conflict. Though the developments in international law have strengthened the legal rights of women, in practice, they remain incompetent. These violations are not the inevitable side effects of the war but intentional war weapons used by armed members or militants. The ongoing Russia-Ukraine crisis has brought to light the atrocities committed by Russian combatants against Ukrainian women in the occupied territories. This research focuses on the cause and consequence of sexual violence against women during armed conflicts and its relation to conditioned stereotypes of society, and further illustrates the International legal framework concerning the issue and its inevitable drawbacks in preventing and protecting the victims and prosecuting the aggressor. This research relies on primary and secondary sources. Though these crimes are serious and fall under the domain of "War Crimes and Crimes against humanity", however, the lack of accountability by the war states, the lack of proper enforcement machinery, and state cooperation in prosecuting the aggressor have further deteriorated the issue, thereby trivializing it.

title: Simple Budgeting Mechanisms with Persistent Private Information
affiliations: University of Georgia - Terry College of Business, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and National Tsing Hua University - Department of Quantitative Finance

detail.title: Simple Budgeting Mechanisms with Persistent Private Information
detail.abstract: We study a dynamic capital budgeting problem in which the division manager possesses persistent private information regarding a project's productivity. The headquarters designs an optimal mechanism to induce truthful reporting from the manager while maximizing its expected payoff from production. Utilizing a combination of assumptions commonly used in the literature, we obtain closed-form solutions to this dynamic adverse selection problem, allowing us to make sharp predictions on how persistent private information distorts capital allocation and production. Despite its dynamic nature, the optimal allocation can be implemented via simple, decentralized, and static mechanisms that do not require the manager to report any private information or the headquarters to track any performance histories. Methodologically, our paper offers a tractable framework that can serve as an off-the-shelf modeling block for future research involving dynamic adverse selection.

title: Executive Autocracy Versus Professional Ethics
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU) - Michael E. Moritz College of Law

detail.title: Executive Autocracy Versus Professional Ethics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am a bar-admitted lawyer and a professor who teaches and writes about professional responsibility, and therefore have -- and champion -- an ethical obligation to support and advance the Constitution, the rule of law, and the professional commitments of the legal profession.

detail.abstract:
During its first year in office, the second Trump Administration has generated abundant evidence to support the claim that it is attempting a radical revision of the functioning of the United States constitutional system and civic space toward Executive autocracy.  That is, virtually unlimited power for the President and his team to act alone, without meaningful checks.  The subjective motives of the administration and its voters vary.  But the trajectory of administration action aligns well with two central elements of autocracy: centralization of power with the leader, and complete subservience of all Executive Branch personnel.  

This essay argues that these aspects of autocracy inherently clash with core ethical commitments of multiple professions of honor: heightened fidelity to the truth, prohibition of participation in wrongful conduct, and analytical independence.  To varying degrees, professions in government service also operate apolitically.  This essay focuses on the professions of law, arms, and intelligence, building on my prior scholarship on these three professions that are especially vital to national security.  

This essay first frames the autocratic drive as reflective of the second term Trump team’s “radical constitutionalism.”  Second, it examines the common core ethical commitments of the professions of law, arms, and intelligence.  Their ethical codes operate as checks against error, illegality, and abuse of authority, and thereby serve the public interest in a republic, especially in the darkest corners of classification where analysis and decision in the Executive Branch often escape effective oversight by the other branches and the public.  These ethical commitments and their functions inevitably clash with attempted Executive autocracy, which to succeed must either purge professionals or else win their acquiescence or de-professionalizing de-ethicalization.  One way to theorize the second Trump Administration’s unprecedented purging, transformation, and personalization of the federal administrative state, this essay argues, is as an attempt to force an exception to professional ethics for Executive Branch service.  This essay concludes by underscoring actionable steps to buttress the professions as a bulwark against authoritarianism, corruption, and disastrous decisions. 

This essay was published as part of an online symposium.  It will be published in print in 2026.

title: The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act, 2018: A Definitive Analysis of Nigerian Competition Law and Regulatory Enforcement
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act, 2018: A Definitive Analysis of Nigerian Competition Law and Regulatory Enforcement
detail.abstract: The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act (FCCPA), 2018, represents a watershed moment in Nigeria's commercial regulatory landscape. The legislation fundamentally reshaped the legal framework governing commercial conduct, moving Nigeria from a fragmented regulatory environment to a unified, specialized structure for competition and consumer protection. This shift was necessary to promote sustainable economic development and secure market integrity. Prior to the FCCPA, regulatory authority over competition matters was diffused and often underdeveloped. The Act explicitly repealed previous laws, most notably the Consumer Protection Council Act, and crucially, sections 118 to 127 of the Investments and Securities Act (ISA) 2007, which had previously vested merger control powers in the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The consolidation of these functions under a single specialized body, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), indicates a strong governmental effort towards professionalizing regulation and promoting transparent enforcement practices. This legal certainty regarding jurisdictional boundaries and compliance requirements is foundational to enhancing investor confidence and attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). The FCCPA itself is a sophisticated piece of legislation, demonstrating international benchmarking. It is modeled, in part, after successful statutes, including the South African Competition Act and principles derived from established EU competition law.

title: The Somatic Marker of Markets: Falsifying Statistical Complexity in Structural Break Detection

detail.title: The Somatic Marker of Markets: Falsifying Statistical Complexity in Structural Break Detection
detail.abstract: Detecting structural breaks in non-stationary, multivariate time series remains a central challenge, particularly under distribution shift. This paper presents a falsification-driven investigation into Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT) inspired approaches to market regime detection. Building on the algorithmic ontology established in [Mak, 2023], we begin by testing a direct predictive analogy: can an Elementary Cellular Automata (ECA) solver, trained on binary-encoded asset returns, forecast market dynamics? This hypothesis is cleanly falsified, revealing fundamental limits of domain transfer. Pivoting to Minimum Description Length (MDL) as a robust segmentation framework, we compare high-resolution multivariate analysis ("The Microscope") against intelligent univariate aggregation ("The Stethoscope"). We demonstrate that high-resolution statistical models (e.g., VAR) are overwhelmed by parameter complexity (Negative MDL Cost), effectively blinding them to the signal. In contrast, the "Coherence Meter"-a hybrid diagnostic that repurposes predictive error as a proxy for systemic rule incoherence-validates the "Somatic Marker Hypothesis": that systemic instability is best detected by measuring the "agony" (predictive failure) of the system rather than modeling its state. In a case study on the Q4 2018 U.S. equity downturn, this Somatic Marker approach detects the regime collapse with 23.9 bits of MDL evidence-twice that of the baseline Stethoscope (11.7 bits). To test for generalizability, we conducted a systematic validation on the Algoplexity Structural Break Benchmark (hosted on Hugging Face). This dual-phase experiment revealed a profound capability: the instrument functions as a powerful early-warning system, detecting instability with a mean lead time of 31.21% in-sample and 39.37% on unseen, out-of-sample data. Our core contribution is a refined "less is more" principle: the final decision framework must be simple and robust, yet powerfully informed by sophisticated, second-order diagnostics.
